messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
# Marcus

Marcus was forty-two when the shortness of breath started. He remembers the date exactly—March 14th, a Tuesday—because it was the morning after his daughter's school recital, an event he'd nearly skipped. He was sitting at his desk in the climate-controlled server room of his firm, staring at lines of code that suddenly seemed to swim before his eyes. His chest tightened. He couldn't draw a full breath. Within hours, the emergency room confirmed what the radiologist's voice on the phone would later make official: Stage III non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. The disease had been growing in his chest cavity for months, pressing against his lungs and heart, and he'd felt nothing until the moment his body simply refused to work properly.

What followed was eighteen months of chemotherapy, radiation, and the specific terror of watching his own mortality become a series of medical appointments. The treatments were brutal. He remembers the oncology suite—the smell of disinfectant and something chemical he couldn't name, the nurse's practiced efficiency as she inserted the central line into his chest, the cold sensation of the needle breaking skin, the way the IV bag dripped poison into his body with the promise that it might save his life. He remembers the CT scanner, the MRI machine, the PET scan, each one a moment of being enclosed in a tube while machines measured whether he was dying faster or slower than before. The breathlessness returned with every scan, not from the disease anymore but from panic—the feeling that he was trapped, that his body was betraying him again, that something unseen was growing inside him that the machines would find.

He survived. The cancer went into remission. But the man who emerged from treatment was not the same. Five years later, Marcus still cannot pass a hospital without his heart rate spiking. The sight of a needle—even in a television commercial, even held by a nurse on a billboard advertisement—triggers a cascade of physical sensation: his shoulders tense, his breathing becomes shallow, and a hot surge of something between fear and anger floods through him. He is certain that his body is still dangerous to him, that the cancer is waiting somewhere in his cells, and that any medical procedure—even a routine blood draw—is the beginning of the end.

He has come to control what he can. His eating has become a careful mathematics: he weighs his portions, counts his calories, monitors his macronutrients with the precision he once applied to database architecture. The control is soothing. When he eats, he eats exactly what he has planned. When he doesn't eat, that too is planned. He has lost fifteen pounds in the past year. His ex-wife mentioned it during a custody exchange. He said nothing.

Exercise is another thing he no longer does. The gym used to be his refuge, but now the exertion triggers the breathlessness, and the breathlessness brings back the panic from the scanner, from the IV line, from the moment in the oncology suite when he understood that his body had turned against him. It is easier not to go. His clothes fit differently now. His back hurts from sitting at his desk all day, but he does not address this because addressing it means seeing a doctor, and seeing a doctor means hospitals, needles, the cold certainty that something is wrong inside him that needs to be found.

He has not had a physical examination in five years. His primary care physician's office calls every six months. He does not return the calls. The thought of sitting in that waiting room, of a nurse taking his blood pressure, of a doctor listening to his chest with a stethoscope and asking him to breathe deeply—the very request to breathe deeply is a trigger now—fills him with a dread so complete that avoidance feels like the only rational choice.

It is his daughter who finally brought him here. She is twelve now, old enough to notice that her father flinches at ambulance sirens, that he has stopped coming to her soccer games because the fields are near the hospital, that he seems always slightly afraid. She asked him, directly, if he was okay. He realized he could not answer honestly. He came to therapy because he could not bear for her to inherit his fear. What he hopes for most is to be able to breathe again without panic. What he fears most is that he will not.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Age discrepancy: The vignette states Marcus was 'forty-two when the shortness of breath started' and 'five years later' he is still struggling. This places him at approximately 47 years old at the time of the vignette. However, the patient demographics indicate age 37. The vignette does not reflect the patient's actual age.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.

He remembers the CT scanner, the MRI machine, the PET scan, each one a moment of being enclosed in a tube while machines measured whether he was dying faster or slower than before. The breathlessness returned with every scan, not from the disease anymore but from panic—the feeling that he was trapped, that his body was betraying him again, that something unseen was growing inside him that the machines would find. His thoughts during those scans were intrusive and uncontrollable: images of the tumor returning, fragments of conversations with his oncologist replaying without warning, the certainty that any scan would reveal the cancer had come back and this time he wouldn't survive it.

His sleep has become fragmented; he wakes at three in the morning with his heart pounding, sometimes without knowing why, other times because he has dreamed of the oncology suite or the scanner's mechanical voice telling him to hold still.

His eating has become a careful mathematics: he weighs his portions, counts his calories, monitors his macronutrients with the precision he once applied to database architecture. It is easier not to go. His clothes fit differently now. His back hurts from sitting at his desk all day, but he does not address this because addressing it means seeing a doctor, and seeing a doctor means hospitals, needles, the cold certainty that something is wrong inside him that needs to be found.

He has not had a physical examination in five years. His primary care physician's office calls every six months. He does not return the calls. The thought of sitting in that waiting room, of a nurse taking his blood pressure, of a doctor listening to his chest with a stethoscope and asking him to breathe deeply—the very request to breathe deeply is a trigger now—fills him with a dread so complete that avoidance feels like the only rational choice. The consequences have accumulated quietly. His work performance has declined; concentration is harder when sleep is fragmented and anxiety is constant. He has missed his daughter's last two soccer seasons because the fields are near the hospital, and the proximity alone is enough to send him into a state of hypervigilance where he cannot focus on anything but the building's location in his peripheral vision. It is his daughter who finally brought him here. She is twelve now, old enough to notice that her father flinches at ambulance sirens, that he has stopped coming to her soccer games, that he seems always slightly afraid. She asked him, directly, if he was okay. He realized he could not answer honestly. He came to therapy because he could not bear for her to inherit his fear. What he hopes for most is to be able to breathe again without panic. What he fears most is that he will not.
